Hi James / team — quick technical answers below. TL;DR: we can stream partial tool_call deltas, and embeddings are billed separately from generation. Example SDK snippets included.

1) Streaming & tool calling— Streaming behavior: when you enable streaming in the SDK, the server emits delta events for both text and structured signals. For chat + tool_call flows we send: 
  - "delta" chunks for partial textual output (same as completions).
  - "tool_call.start": emitted when the model begins a tool invocation (you'll receive the tool name and an id).
  - "tool_call.delta": partial args/content for that tool_call as they are generated.
  - "tool_call.end": full args + a finalization signal.

This means your UI can render an in-progress tool pane as soon as the first tool_call.start/delta arrives. For strict JSON-schema enforcement we recommend post-processing the final tool_call.end payload to validate against the schema before executing.

2) Token accounting— Prompts + context tokens are counted toward request tokens; generation tokens (the model output) are counted as response tokens. Billing shows both prompt and completion tokens for generation calls. Embedding calls are billed per-vector (separately) and are not billed as generation tokens, though they have their own per-request cost.

Practical guidance: always estimate total tokens as: token(prompt) + max_tokens you permit for completion. If you pass max_tokens=256, plan for that in cost estimates even if you think the model will stop earlier. Use stop sequences to keep completions short when appropriate. For chat usage, note that the entire conversation history included in the request contributes to prompt tokens; consider token-limited rolling context or summarization for long histories.

3) Chat vs completions recommendation— Use chat endpoints for multi-turn interactions, tool-calling, and structured JSON outputs (it has explicit tooling hooks and structured output semantics). Completions can be used for single-shot generation or where you control prompt formatting tightly. Both support streaming and stop sequences but chat provides better primitives for tool_call events and message role semantics.

4) Embeddings & reranker pattern— Typical flow we recommend:
  - Candidate generation: search or shortlist docs via boolean filters or metadata.
  - Embedding lookup: compute embeddings for query and candidates (these calls are billed as embedding requests).
  - ANN fetch: retrieve nearest neighbors in vector DB (not a token operation).
  - Rerank: run a lightweight cross-encoder/generation prompt to score top N candidates via the chat endpoint (this is a generation call and will bill tokens).

5) SDK/auth snippet (pseudo-code, pasteable):

// NodeJS example (redwood-sdk)
const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, region: 'us-west-2', streaming: true });

// streaming chat call with tool calling enabled
const stream = await client.chat.stream({
  model: 'redwood-chat-1',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Find the best three policies for data retention in EU.' }],
  tools: [{ name: 'policy_lookup', schema: /* JSON schema */ }],
  max_tokens: 256,
  stop: ['\n\n']
});

for await (const chunk of stream) {
  if (chunk.type === 'tool_call.start') { renderToolPaneStart(chunk.tool); }
  if (chunk.type === 'tool_call.delta') { appendToolArgs(chunk.argsChunk); }
  if (chunk.type === 'tool_call.end') { validateAndExecuteTool(chunk.fullArgs); }
  if (chunk.type === 'delta') { appendToMainStream(chunk.content); }
}

Auth notes: for hosted API we recommend short-lived API keys rotated regularly and a server-side credential exchange. For Private deployments, mTLS or client certs + KMS-backed key management are supported.
